questions.title: Lung development and antenatally diagnosed CPAM
questions.body_md:
Marks: 3 + 3 + 4
Describe briefly the stages of development of the lung. Discuss the different classifications for congenital cystic adenomatoid malformations (CCAM) of the lung. Briefly outline the management of antenatally diagnosed CCAM.

### (a) Lung development - 3 marks

The respiratory diverticulum arises from ventral foregut endoderm at approximately four weeks. Endoderm forms the airway epithelium and glands; surrounding splanchnic mesoderm provides connective tissue, smooth muscle, cartilage and pulmonary vessels. Separation from the oesophagus and repeated branching establish the bronchial tree. Developmental phases overlap, and their gestational boundaries vary slightly among texts.

| Phase | Approximate timing | Main events |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Embryonic | 4-7 weeks | Lung bud, trachea, main bronchi and initial lobar/segmental pattern. |
| Pseudoglandular | 5-17 weeks | Conducting airways branch to terminal bronchioles; no effective gas-exchange units. |
| Canalicular | 16-25 weeks | Respiratory bronchioles develop; capillary network expands; epithelial differentiation and early surfactant production begin. |
| Saccular | 24 weeks to birth | Terminal saccules enlarge; interstitium thins; type II cells increase surfactant and type I cells form a thin exchange surface. |
| Alveolar | Late fetal life through childhood | Secondary septation and microvascular maturation progressively increase alveolar number and surface area. |

Surfactant production begins before the lung is functionally mature. Viability cannot be assigned to a single phase or week: airway development, surfactant, vascular maturation and neonatal support all matter. The alveolar phase continues well beyond birth.

### (b) CPAM classifications - 3 marks

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) is the preferred term for the lesion historically called CCAM. It is abnormal development of terminal airways with disordered proliferation and cyst formation. Histological type and prenatal ultrasound morphology answer different questions and must be stated separately.

| Stocker type | Characteristic level/pattern | Exam relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Tracheobronchial; very small cysts in diffusely abnormal lungs | Rare, often severe and incompatible with normal gas exchange. |
| 1 | Bronchial/bronchiolar; one or more large cysts, typically >2 cm | Commonest pattern; ciliated epithelial lining and possible mucinous cell clusters. |
| 2 | Bronchiolar; multiple smaller cysts, usually <2 cm | Associated congenital anomalies may determine prognosis. |
| 3 | Bronchiolar/alveolar duct; tiny cysts giving a solid gross appearance | Large lesions can cause marked mediastinal displacement. |
| 4 | Distal acinar/alveolar; large peripheral thin-walled cysts | Can mimic cystic pleuropulmonary blastoma; careful pathology and clinical assessment are needed. |

The original Stocker system comprised types I-III; the expanded system includes types 0-IV. Prenatal classification describes macrocystic lesions with sonographically visible cysts (commonly using a 5 mm threshold), microcystic/echogenic lesions and mixed lesions. A 5 mm ultrasound threshold is not the 2 cm pathological distinction between types 1 and 2. Doppler identification of a systemic feeding artery suggests sequestration or a hybrid lesion.

### (c) Antenatal management - 4 marks

Confirm the lesion by expert ultrasound, assess anatomy and fetal cardiac function, and look for mediastinal shift, polyhydramnios and hydrops. Use Doppler to define vascular supply. MRI can clarify anatomy, remaining lung and late gestation mass effect when it will change delivery planning.

Calculate CPAM volume ratio: CVR = (length x width x height x 0.52) / head circumference, using consistent centimetre measurements. Follow the trend, cyst pattern and fetal physiology. CVR above approximately 1.6 identifies higher hydrops risk but is not, by itself, an instruction to operate. A dominant cyst may cause deterioration even at a lower ratio.

A stable fetus without hydrops usually undergoes serial ultrasound and planned delivery. Large or growing lesions, hydrops or significant compression require a specialist fetal centre. Maternal betamethasone is considered particularly for high-risk microcystic lesions. A dominant macrocyst producing hydrops or major compression may benefit from thoracoamniotic drainage. Fetal surgery is exceptional rescue treatment in highly selected cases; gestation, response to steroids and maternal risks govern the decision.

Plan delivery where neonatal ventilation, paediatric surgery and escalation are available if the lesion is large or symptomatic risk is high. Caesarean section or EXIT is reserved for specific obstetric or anticipated cardiopulmonary indications. After birth, stabilize the infant and obtain cross-sectional imaging as appropriate. Apparent prenatal regression does not prove disappearance. Symptomatic lesions generally require resection; elective surgery versus structured surveillance for an asymptomatic lesion is a counselling decision with variable practice.

Exam emphasis: name both classification systems, write the CVR formula, and divide management into uncomplicated surveillance, fetal compromise and postnatal planning.

### References
- [Original histopathology series, modified Stocker classification](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8637997/)
- [APSA Fetal Diagnosis and Treatment Committee, CPAM Prenatal Counseling Series (2018)](https://apsapedsurg.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/APSA-CPAM-Brochure_FNL.pdf)
- [Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, CPAM clinical overview](https://www.chop.edu/conditions-diseases/congenital-cystic-adenomatoid-malformation-ccam)
- [Connecticut Children's Fetal Care Center, CPAM management](https://www.connecticutchildrens.org/specialties-conditions/fetal-care-center/fetal-care-medical-professionals/congenital-pulmonary-airway-malformation-medical-professionals)

### Illustration
CPAM: risk assessment and treatment branches
CVR = (length x width x height x 0.52) / head circumference. Cyst size on prenatal ultrasound and Stocker histology are different classifications. Exceptional fetal rescue surgery requires individualized specialist selection.

questions.title: Chemotherapy: mechanisms, toxicities and febrile neutropenia
questions.body_md:
Marks: 4 + 4 + 2
Outline the mechanism of actions of different chemotherapeutic drugs used for solid tumors in children. Enumerate their specific toxicities. Describe briefly the management of febrile neutropenia in a child receiving chemotherapy?

### (a) Mechanisms and representative use - 4 marks

Paediatric solid-tumour chemotherapy uses combinations of agents with different mechanisms and resistance patterns. Treatment is tumour-, stage- and protocol-specific. The following are representative drugs rather than a list of interchangeable regimens; doses and scheduling require an oncology protocol.

| Class / drug | Mechanism | Representative paediatric use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alkylators: cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide | Reactive metabolites cross-link DNA and impair replication. | Sarcomas, neuroblastoma and other protocol-defined solid tumours. |
| Platinum: cisplatin, carboplatin | Intra- and interstrand DNA cross-links. | Germ-cell tumours, hepatoblastoma, neuroblastoma; carboplatin in selected retinoblastoma protocols. |
| Vinca alkaloid: vincristine | Inhibits microtubule assembly and arrests mitosis. | Wilms tumour, rhabdomyosarcoma and neuroblastoma combinations. |
| Anthracycline: doxorubicin | Topoisomerase II inhibition, DNA intercalation and oxidative injury. | Selected Wilms tumour, sarcoma and neuroblastoma regimens. |
| Dactinomycin | Intercalates DNA and suppresses RNA synthesis. | Wilms tumour and rhabdomyosarcoma. |
| Etoposide | Inhibits topoisomerase II, producing DNA strand breaks. | Germ-cell tumours, neuroblastoma and Ewing sarcoma. |
| Irinotecan / topotecan | Inhibit topoisomerase I. | Selected relapsed or high-risk solid-tumour protocols. |
| Methotrexate | Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and folate-dependent nucleotide synthesis. | High-dose treatment in osteosarcoma, with leucovorin rescue. |
| Bleomycin | Metal-dependent free-radical injury produces DNA breaks. | Selected germ-cell tumour protocols. |
| Busulfan / melphalan | Alkylating DNA damage. | Selected high-dose consolidation with stem-cell rescue. |

### (b) Specific toxicities and prevention - 4 marks

| Drug | Characteristic toxicity | Monitoring / prevention principle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cyclophosphamide | Myelosuppression, haemorrhagic cystitis, gonadal injury; high-dose cardiac toxicity. | Hydration, mesna when indicated, urine monitoring and fertility discussion. |
| Ifosfamide | Cystitis, encephalopathy and renal tubular injury/Fanconi syndrome. | Mesna and hydration protect the bladder, not the renal tubule; check renal function and electrolytes. |
| Cisplatin | Nephrotoxicity, magnesium wasting, ototoxicity, neuropathy and emesis. | Renal/electrolyte assessment, hydration and audiology; antiemetic support. |
| Carboplatin | Myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia; hypersensitivity. | CBC and exposure/renal-based protocol dosing; less renal/ear toxicity than cisplatin, not zero. |
| Vincristine | Peripheral/autonomic neuropathy, constipation or ileus, SIADH. | Neurological and bowel review; intravenous only: intrathecal administration is fatal. |
| Doxorubicin | Cumulative cardiomyopathy and vesicant injury. | Baseline/serial cardiac assessment and cumulative-dose record; dexrazoxane in appropriate protocols. |
| Dactinomycin | Mucositis, myelosuppression, hepatic injury including sinusoidal obstruction; radiation enhancement. | Liver tests and coordination with radiotherapy. |
| Etoposide | Myelosuppression, infusion hypotension and therapy-related leukaemia. | CBC, prescribed infusion rate and long-term follow-up. |
| Irinotecan / topotecan | Irinotecan: early cholinergic symptoms and delayed diarrhoea; topotecan: marked myelosuppression. | Recognize early versus delayed diarrhoea; hydration and protocol-specific treatment. |
| Methotrexate | Mucositis, myelosuppression, nephrotoxicity and delayed clearance. | Hydration, urine alkalinization, drug levels and timed leucovorin; rescue escalation for severe delayed clearance. |
| Bleomycin | Pneumonitis/fibrosis, skin changes and fever; relatively little marrow suppression. | Assess lung/renal risk; communicate exposure to anaesthesia and avoid unnecessary hyperoxia without withholding needed oxygen. |
| High-dose busulfan / melphalan | Profound marrow suppression, mucositis; busulfan also seizures and sinusoidal obstruction. | Stem-cell support and protocol-specific prophylaxis/monitoring. |

Most cytotoxic regimens also cause infection risk, nausea, mucosal damage and alopecia. Tumour lysis, nutritional deficits and extravasation require separate assessment. A toxicity-prevention measure must be linked to the correct organ: mesna prevents urothelial injury, while leucovorin rescues normal tissue after methotrexate.

### (c) Febrile neutropenia - 2 marks

Common definitions use a single temperature >=38.3 C or >=38.0 C sustained for one hour with ANC <500/microlitre, or expected to fall below that level. Local paediatric oncology definitions vary. Treat suspected febrile neutropenia as an emergency; do not wait for the blood count in an unwell child.

Assess airway, breathing, perfusion and sepsis; obtain CBC, renal function and blood cultures from each central-line lumen, plus peripheral cultures when feasible. Cultures must not delay antibiotics. Give prompt empiric IV antipseudomonal therapy, for example cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam according to local resistance and allergy guidance. Reserve additional aminoglycoside/glycopeptide coverage for instability, resistant organisms or a defined indication.

Provide source-directed investigation, fluid/vasoactive support when required and urgent oncology/PICU input. Avoid rectal examination and rectal temperature measurement. Use validated risk assessment for any outpatient pathway. Persistent fever in a stable child alone does not mandate broader antibiotics; prolonged high-risk episodes require reassessment for invasive fungal disease. These latter principles reflect the 2023 update, published after this examination.

### References
- [Cancer Care Ontario, vincristine monograph](https://www.cancercareontario.ca/en/drugformulary/drugs/monograph/43891)
- [Cancer Care Ontario, cisplatin monograph](https://www.cancercareontario.ca/en/drugformulary/drugs/monograph/43896)
- [Cancer Care Ontario, ifosfamide monograph](https://www.cancercareontario.ca/en/drugformulary/drugs/monograph/44231)
- [COG-endorsed paediatric fever/neutropenia guideline (2023)](https://childrensoncologygroup.org/docs/default-source/pdf/COG_SC_FN_Guideline_Document.pdf)
- [RCH, fever and suspected or confirmed neutropenia](https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Fever_and_suspected_or_confirmed_neutropenia/)

### Illustration
Anticancer drugs: target and sentinel toxicity
Top panels summarize drug-target associations; they do not represent a sequential treatment regimen. Bottom branch is the emergency response to possible febrile neutropenia. Mesna does not prevent ifosfamide tubular toxicity.

questions.title: Paediatric GCS, Paediatric Trauma Score and ISS
questions.body_md:
Marks: 4 + 3 + 3
Describe the Pediatric Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and Pediatric Trauma Score (PTS). Define Injury Severity Score (ISS) for patients with multiple traumas?

### (a) Paediatric Glasgow Coma Scale - 4 marks

GCS describes consciousness using eye opening, best verbal response and best motor response. The total ranges from 3 to 15. Use developmentally appropriate language and behaviour for preverbal children; state which paediatric version is being used. Record the components, for example E3 V4 M5 = 12, and the examination time, rather than only a total.

| Component | Response in a young child | Score |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eyes | Spontaneous / to voice / to pain / none | 4 / 3 / 2 / 1 |
| Verbal | Age-appropriate words, interaction or social smile; fixes/follows | 5 |
| Verbal | Cries but is consolable; fewer words than usual | 4 |
| Verbal | Persistently irritable cry | 3 |
| Verbal | Moans to pain | 2 |
| Verbal | No response | 1 |
| Motor | Normal spontaneous purposeful movement or obeys commands | 6 |
| Motor | Localizes painful stimulus | 5 |
| Motor | Withdraws from pain / normal flexion | 4 |
| Motor | Abnormal flexion | 3 |
| Motor | Extension | 2 |
| Motor | No response | 1 |

In a verbal older child, V5 is oriented conversation, V4 confused conversation, V3 inappropriate words, V2 incomprehensible sounds and V1 none; M6 is obeying commands. The table uses the RCH developmental adaptation. Other accepted infant scales use slightly different descriptions: do not combine incompatible versions in one scoring table.

Assess the best observed response after initial resuscitation and repeat serially. Document unequal limb responses separately. Sedatives, neuromuscular blockade, hypoxia, shock, seizures, developmental disability, facial swelling and intubation can make a component uninterpretable. Mark it not testable with the reason; an untestable verbal score should not be presented as a reliable numerical total.

Typical head-injury bands are mild 13-15, moderate 9-12 and severe <=8. A score <=8 after resuscitation prompts urgent expert airway and neuroprotective assessment. Deterioration, pupil changes or focal findings matter even when the total remains high. GCS is neither a substitute for the primary survey nor a stand-alone CT or airway rule.

### (b) Paediatric Trauma Score - 3 marks

PTS is a six-item paediatric triage score combining size, physiology and anatomical injury. Each item receives +2, +1 or -1; sum the six items for a total from -6 to +12. The categories below are the conventional examination formulation.

| Item | +2 | +1 | -1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Weight | >20 kg | 10-20 kg | <10 kg |
| Airway | Normal | Maintainable with simple support | Unmaintainable |
| Systolic BP | >90 mmHg | 50-90 mmHg | <50 mmHg |
| CNS | Awake | Obtunded / altered | Coma |
| Open wounds | None | Minor | Major or penetrating |
| Skeletal injury | None | Closed fracture | Open or multiple fractures |

Lower values indicate greater injury severity. PTS <=8 conventionally supports referral to a paediatric trauma service. Its fixed blood-pressure bands are a scoring convention, not modern age-specific definitions of shock. The weight item intentionally lowers the score in small children, so an otherwise normal small child does not automatically score 12. Use local trauma activation criteria alongside it.

### (c) Injury Severity Score - 3 marks

ISS is an anatomical summary of multiple trauma based on Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) coding. AIS grades individual injuries from 1 (minor) to 6 (maximal). It requires the appropriate AIS dictionary and trained coding; examples of grades should not be guessed from bedside impressions.

Allocate injuries to six ISS regions: (1) head/neck, (2) face, (3) chest, (4) abdomen/pelvic contents, (5) extremities/pelvic girdle and (6) external. Select the highest AIS grade in each region. Take the three highest grades from three different regions, square each and add: ISS = A squared + B squared + C squared.

Worked arithmetic: if the highest regional grades are head 4, chest 3 and abdomen 2, ISS = 16 + 9 + 4 = 29. This demonstrates the calculation only, not how to assign injury codes. ISS ranges from 0 to 75; any AIS 6 injury makes ISS 75. ISS >15 is a common major-trauma definition, although reporting thresholds vary.

ISS supports audit, research and case-mix comparison rather than immediate resuscitation decisions. It ignores additional severe injuries within the same region and may only be final after investigation. NISS instead squares the three most severe individual injuries irrespective of region. GCS measures neurological response, PTS aids triage and ISS summarizes anatomical injury: these functions are complementary.

### References
- [RCH Trauma Manual, head injury and paediatric GCS](https://www.rch.org.au/trauma-service/manual/head-injury/)
- [NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation, injury scoring](https://aci.health.nsw.gov.au/networks/trauma/data/injury-scoring)
- [CDC, field triage report and ISS definition](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr5801a1.htm)
- [OSF Region I EMS, paediatric scoring reference](https://osf-p-001.sitecorecontenthub.cloud/api/public/content/ae7178a96b254bbdb77f25981a6ef4f1?v=fc03a36d)

### Illustration
GCS, PTS and ISS answer different questions
GCS developmental wording must match the chosen scale. PTS blood-pressure bands are score categories rather than age-specific shock thresholds. ISS is usually finalized after injury characterization.

questions.title: Childhood germ-cell tumours: origin, pathology and markers
questions.body_md:
Marks: 3 + 4 + 3
Discuss Germ cell tumors in children under the following sub-headings: (a) Embryogenesis. (b) Pathological types. (c) Tumour markers for diagnosis and management.

### (a) Embryogenesis - 3 marks

Primordial germ cells arise from an early pluripotent cell lineage and are temporarily found in the wall of the yolk sac near the allantois. During early embryonic development they migrate through the hindgut/dorsal mesentery region to the developing genital ridges. They subsequently differentiate in the gonadal environment into the germ-cell lineages.

Failure of appropriate migration, survival or differentiation provides a developmental explanation for many extragonadal germ-cell tumours. Their characteristic distribution includes sacrococcygeal, retroperitoneal, mediastinal and intracranial midline sites. This is a useful embryological model, not proof that every tumour originates by the same mechanism. Gonadal and extragonadal tumours are biologically heterogeneous.

An undifferentiated germ-cell phenotype produces germinoma-pattern tumours: seminoma in the testis and dysgerminoma in the ovary. Embryonal carcinoma retains pluripotent embryonal characteristics. Somatic differentiation yields teratoma; extraembryonic differentiation yields yolk-sac tumour or choriocarcinoma. Mixed tumours contain more than one component.

Prepubertal and postpubertal tumours differ in site, histology and molecular pathways. Sacrococcygeal teratoma is prominent in neonates, while adolescent gonadal disease more closely resembles adult-type tumours. Testicular germ-cell neoplasia in situ is relevant to many postpubertal tumours, but is not a universal precursor for childhood yolk-sac tumour or teratoma.

### (b) Pathological types - 4 marks

| Type | Characteristic pathology | Clinical / marker association |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mature teratoma | Well-differentiated somatic tissues, potentially from all three germ layers. | Often benign in young children; assess completeness of resection and site. |
| Immature teratoma | Embryonic immature tissue, classically neuroepithelium, graded by extent. | Immaturity alone is not synonymous with a malignant yolk-sac component; management is age/site dependent. |
| Yolk-sac tumour | Reticular/microcystic patterns; Schiller-Duval bodies and eosinophilic globules may occur. | Common malignant component in young children; AFP is usually elevated. |
| Embryonal carcinoma | Primitive pleomorphic epithelial cells in solid, glandular or papillary patterns. | Often a component of mixed adolescent tumours; AFP and/or beta-hCG may rise. |
| Choriocarcinoma | Cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with haemorrhage and necrosis. | Marked beta-hCG; aggressive haematogenous spread. |
| Seminoma / dysgerminoma / germinoma | Relatively uniform large cells with clear cytoplasm, fibrous septa and lymphocytes. | Same broad family at different sites; AFP should not be elevated from a pure lesion. |
| Mixed malignant GCT | Two or more histological components. | Marker profile reflects the secreting components; specimen sampling must be adequate. |
| Teratoma with somatic-type malignancy | A somatic malignant component, such as sarcoma, arises in a teratoma. | Rare; requires expert pathology and component-specific planning. |

Pathology should report all components, margins and relevant grade. Histological confirmation, imaging and marker interpretation together establish the diagnosis and stage. A normal marker panel does not exclude teratoma, germinoma-pattern tumour or another non-secreting malignant component.

### (c) Tumour markers - 3 marks

AFP is produced predominantly by yolk-sac elements, with possible contribution from embryonal carcinoma. Interpret it against age-specific infant reference ranges: physiological neonatal AFP can be high and normally falls with age. Its serum half-life is approximately 5-7 days. Beta-hCG is secreted by trophoblastic elements and some embryonal or germinoma-pattern tumours; its half-life is approximately 1-2 days. LDH is a nonspecific indicator of tumour burden and turnover, not a diagnostic discriminator.

Obtain baseline AFP and beta-hCG before treatment when possible. Use serial levels to assess response and surveillance, comparing decline with expected kinetics. Failure to fall appropriately, plateau or a confirmed new rise may indicate persistent or recurrent secreting disease and requires imaging/clinical correlation. A single early rise may reflect treatment-related release, and results can be affected by assay or non-tumour causes.

AFP elevation in a tumour labelled pure seminoma/dysgerminoma should trigger review for an occult nonseminomatous component or a separate explanation. Conversely, normal markers cannot establish complete remission in a non-secreting tumour. Modern miRNA biomarkers remain an evolving area in paediatric practice and do not replace standard markers.

Exam emphasis: link embryonic differentiation to histology, and histology to markers; state infant AFP physiology and both marker half-lives. Avoid classifying every immature teratoma as malignant or every marker-negative lesion as benign.

### References
- [National Cancer Institute, Childhood Extracranial Germ Cell Tumors Treatment (PDQ), health professional version](https://www.cancer.gov/types/extracranial-germ-cell/hp/germ-cell-treatment-pdq)

### Illustration
Germ-cell differentiation and marker associations
This is a differentiation concept, not a complete molecular lineage tree. Mixed components can coexist. Normal markers do not exclude a non-secreting tumour; raised AFP is inconsistent with an otherwise pure germinoma-pattern tumour unless explained separately.

questions.title: Paediatric renal transplantation
questions.body_md:
Marks: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2
Discuss pediatric renal transplantation under the following sub-headings: (a) Indications. (b) Types. (c) Pre-operative assessment. (d) Immunosuppressant drugs required.

### (a) Indications - 3 marks

Kidney transplantation is the preferred kidney replacement therapy for a suitable child with irreversible kidney failure. It aims to improve survival, growth, development and quality of life compared with prolonged dialysis. Referral should begin early enough to investigate the cause of kidney failure, prepare the lower urinary tract and evaluate a donor before urgent replacement becomes necessary.

Common underlying disorders include congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (renal dysplasia/hypoplasia, obstructive uropathy and reflux-associated damage), hereditary nephropathies and cystic disease, glomerular diseases and selected metabolic disorders. The diagnosis matters because disease recurrence and extra-renal manifestations may alter transplant strategy.

Indications are progressive irreversible failure with inadequate filtration and/or refractory uraemic symptoms, growth/nutritional impairment, electrolyte or acid-base disturbance, fluid overload or hypertension despite appropriate management. KDIGO recommends considering pre-emptive transplantation in children when eGFR is <15 mL/min/1.73 m2, or earlier with symptoms, provided suitability and timing are established. This is not a requirement to wait for symptomatic uraemia.

Temporary reasons to defer include uncontrolled active infection, active malignancy and unresolved major medical or psychosocial barriers. These require correction and reassessment rather than automatic permanent exclusion. An abnormal bladder or young age alone is not a contraindication if safe drainage, surgical feasibility and long-term care can be achieved.

### (b) Types and operative approaches - 3 marks

| Classification | Types | Practical significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Donor source | Living related; living unrelated; deceased donor (donation after brain death or circulatory death where available). | Living donation permits planned timing and often shorter cold ischaemia; donor safety is independently assessed. |
| Timing | Pre-emptive; after peritoneal dialysis or haemodialysis. | Pre-emptive transplantation avoids dialysis exposure when feasible; dialysis may provide an essential bridge. |
| Graft / anatomy | Single kidney; selected en-bloc paediatric donor grafts. | Donor-recipient size, vessel calibre and thrombosis risk influence selection. |
| Compatibility pathway | ABO-compatible and crossmatch-compatible standard pathway; selected incompatible or paired-exchange pathways. | Incompatible transplantation requires specialist selection, additional treatment and risk counselling. |
| Placement | Usually heterotopic, extraperitoneal iliac fossa in larger children; modified intra-abdominal/retroperitoneal placement in small recipients. | Vascular anastomosis site and approach depend on recipient size and donor vessels. |

A renal allograft is the usual transplant: an autotransplant is relocation of the child's own kidney for selected vascular/urological indications and does not replace transplantation for end-stage bilateral failure. In a small recipient, adult-sized graft perfusion and fluid requirements demand coordinated anaesthetic and intensive care planning.

### (c) Pre-operative assessment - 2 marks

Recipient assessment includes the cause and trajectory of kidney disease, growth and nutrition, blood pressure, cardiac status, vascular access/anatomy, previous abdominal surgery, coagulation, infection and vaccination review. Assess recurrence risk, thrombosis history, sensitizing events, ABO group, HLA typing, donor-specific antibodies and crossmatch. Screen infection risks such as CMV, EBV, hepatitis, HIV and tuberculosis according to age, exposure and local policy.

Evaluate urinary drainage deliberately: history of UTI/continence and catheterization, ultrasound and selected VCUG or urodynamics for valve bladder, neurogenic dysfunction, reflux or prior reconstruction. Establish a low-pressure reservoir with dependable emptying before exposing the graft to it. CIC, bowel care and selected reconstruction are individualized. Native nephrectomy is selective, not routine: consider uncontrolled infection, severe protein loss, refractory hypertension or another specific indication.

Assess donor health separately, confirm informed consent and prepare the family for lifelong medication, drug monitoring and follow-up. Adolescents need a practical adherence and transition plan. Review transport, medication access, schooling, fertility and eventual adult care.

### (d) Immunosuppression - 2 marks

| Phase | Representative drugs | Purpose / important toxicity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Induction | Basiliximab; anti-thymocyte globulin in selected higher-risk recipients; perioperative corticosteroid. | Prevent early rejection; choice balances immunological risk against infection and cytopenias. |
| Maintenance | Tacrolimus (or ciclosporin) + mycophenolate + corticosteroid, with centre-specific steroid minimization in selected children. | Calcineurin inhibition suppresses T-cell activation; mycophenolate inhibits lymphocyte purine synthesis. |
| Alternatives | Azathioprine; selected mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus/everolimus. | Used for defined indications; mTOR agents may impair wound healing and cause proteinuria/dyslipidaemia. |
| Acute rejection treatment | Pulse corticosteroid for suitable cellular rejection; lymphocyte-depleting or antibody-directed therapies as indicated by biopsy and mechanism. | Rescue treatment is distinct from routine maintenance and must follow transplant-team assessment. |

Monitor calcineurin-inhibitor levels and renal function, BP/glucose, CBC, infection and graft status. Tacrolimus can cause nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity and diabetes; mycophenolate causes gastrointestinal symptoms and marrow suppression and is teratogenic. Steroids affect growth, bone and metabolism. Infection prophylaxis, vaccination planning and EBV-related lymphoproliferative risk accompany immunosuppression. Exact regimens vary; later paediatric guidance should be read alongside the 2022 examination framework.

### References
- [KDIGO, transplant candidate guideline (2020)](https://kdigo.org/guidelines/transplant-candidate/)
- [KDIGO, transplant recipient guideline (2009; adults and children)](https://kdigo.org/guidelines/transplant-recipient/)
- [European paediatric kidney transplant immunosuppression guideline (2026; later update)](https://doi.org/10.1097/TP.0000000000005772)

### Illustration
Paediatric kidney transplant: prepare both graft and recipient
Pre-emptive means before dialysis, not before evaluation. Bladder dysfunction must be made safe; it is not automatically a transplant contraindication. Induction and maintenance agents are selected by the transplant team.

questions.title: Neonatal shock: recognition and management
questions.body_md:
Marks: 2 + 3 + 5
Discuss neonatal shock under the following sub-headings: (a) Types. (b) Diagnosis. (c) Protocol for management.

### (a) Types - 2 marks

Shock is inadequate effective tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery for metabolic needs. Neonates can have more than one mechanism simultaneously; hypotension is neither necessary for early shock nor sufficient to define its cause. Classify by the failing part of the circulation.

| Type | Mechanism | Neonatal examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hypovolaemic | Reduced preload / circulating volume. | Placental or internal haemorrhage, dehydration, gastrointestinal loss, operative loss. |
| Distributive | Abnormal vascular tone and maldistribution. | Sepsis; less commonly anaphylaxis. Capillary leak can add relative hypovolaemia. |
| Cardiogenic | Pump failure or structural flow failure. | Asphyxial myocardial dysfunction, myocarditis, arrhythmia, critical congenital heart disease. |
| Obstructive | Mechanical impediment to cardiac filling or output. | Tension pneumothorax, tamponade; critical pulmonary vascular obstruction/PPHN physiology. |
| Mixed | Several mechanisms coexist. | Sepsis with myocardial depression, NEC with sepsis and third-space loss. |

### (b) Diagnosis - 3 marks

Suspect shock with poor feeding, lethargy, apnoea, abnormal temperature, tachycardia or late bradycardia, weak pulses, prolonged capillary refill, cool/mottled skin, altered consciousness and reduced urine output. Some septic infants have warm extremities and bounding pulses. Assess trends, gestation, postnatal age and the clinical context.

Measure BP with an appropriate cuff and consider invasive monitoring when indicated. A mean pressure below gestational age in weeks is a commonly used screening heuristic in premature infants, not a treatment threshold that replaces perfusion assessment. Compare pre- and postductal saturations and femoral versus upper-limb pulses when cardiac disease is possible.

Immediate bedside glucose and blood gas/lactate help identify reversible metabolic problems and monitor response. Obtain CBC, electrolytes, calcium, renal function, cultures and coagulation tests as appropriate without delaying treatment. Early haemoglobin can underestimate acute blood loss. Chest imaging/ultrasound may identify pneumothorax or lung disease; targeted echocardiography assesses ventricular function, shunts, filling, ductal dependence and pulmonary hypertension.

Follow urine output, lactate trend and acid-base status alongside examination. A normal lactate does not exclude early shock; a raised lactate is not specific for sepsis. Do not transfer an unstable infant for CT before treating a readily reversible bedside cause.

### (c) Management protocol - 5 marks

1. Call neonatal/PICU help, maintain temperature, secure the airway and provide oxygen/ventilation appropriate to the physiology. Monitor ECG, saturations and frequent BP; obtain IV access or umbilical venous access where appropriate. Intraosseous access is a rescue option with neonatal expertise. Correct hypoglycaemia promptly and monitor glucose and calcium.

2. Search for an immediately reversible cause while supporting circulation. Decompress a clinically suspected tension pneumothorax without waiting for a radiograph. Control haemorrhage and prepare blood products. In an infant with poor systemic perfusion, weak femoral pulses or differential saturations, consider duct-dependent heart disease; arrange urgent echocardiography and prostaglandin E1 under specialist direction, anticipating apnoea.

3. If hypovolaemia is likely, give an initial 10 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid aliquot, then reassess perfusion, BP, lung findings and liver size before further fluid. Use blood promptly for significant haemorrhage. Administration speed and further volume depend on gestation and cause; premature infants, myocardial dysfunction and congenital heart disease require particular caution. Avoid serial automatic boluses in a nonresponding infant.

4. If sepsis is possible, obtain cultures when feasible and administer empiric IV antibiotics promptly according to neonatal onset, local resistance, line/abdominal source and meningitis risk. Support source control, for example drainage or urgent surgical treatment of perforation. Diagnostic procedures such as lumbar puncture must wait if the infant is unstable.

5. Persistent impaired perfusion after appropriate preload assessment needs early vasoactive support and echocardiographic reassessment. An inotrope is considered for myocardial dysfunction; a vasopressor for low vascular tone. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine or dobutamine are selected according to physiology and local neonatal protocols rather than BP alone. Dopamine can raise BP without reliably improving systemic flow. Refractory shock requires assessment for ongoing loss, obstruction, adrenal insufficiency or metabolic disease; hydrocortisone is reserved for selected refractory cases.

Reassess after every intervention: mental state, pulse quality, capillary refill, urine output, lactate/acid-base trend, oxygenation and cardiac function. A urine output around >=1 mL/kg/hour is a useful ongoing target once transition and renal context are considered. Correct the cause of acidosis; bicarbonate is not routine treatment for shock. Arrange safe specialist transfer and communicate fluid totals, drug infusions and response.

Exam emphasis: recognition precedes hypotension; initial fluid is a reassessed aliquot, not an automatic large cumulative volume; consider sepsis, haemorrhage, pneumothorax and ductal closure in parallel.

### References
- [RCH, neonatal intravenous fluids and shock aliquots](https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Neonatal_intravenous_fluids/)
- [Safer Care Victoria, cyanosed neonate and duct-dependent disease](https://www.safercare.vic.gov.au/best-practice-improvement/clinical-guidance/neonatal/cyanosed-neonate-assessment)
- [Resuscitation Council UK, newborn transition guidance (2025; birth-specific context)](https://www.resus.org.uk/professional-library/2025-resuscitation-guidelines/newborn-resuscitation-and-support-transition-infants-birth)

### Illustration
Neonatal shock: stabilize and identify the mechanism
The branches are concurrent considerations, not a requirement to finish fluid treatment before investigating sepsis or heart disease. Hypotension can be late; prematurity and myocardial dysfunction increase the need for cautious fluid reassessment.

questions.title: Bladder innervation and neurogenic bladder pharmacotherapy
questions.body_md:
Marks: 5 + 5
Discuss the innervation of the urinary bladder and the external urinary sphincter. Classify and enumerate the various drugs used for pharmacological management of neurogenic bladder and discuss briefly the mechanism of action of these drugs.

### (a) Innervation and coordination - 5 marks

Normal continence requires a compliant low-pressure reservoir, a competent outlet and coordinated voluntary emptying. The bladder wall is smooth muscle; the external urethral sphincter is striated muscle. Sacral spinal reflexes are coordinated by supraspinal networks, particularly the pontine micturition centre, periaqueductal grey and cortical pathways.

| Pathway | Origin / nerve | Main action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parasympathetic | Sacral S2-S4 via pelvic nerves. | Acetylcholine activates detrusor muscarinic receptors, especially functional M3 receptors, to produce contraction. |
| Sympathetic | Thoracolumbar, approximately T11-L2, via hypogastric pathways. | Beta-3 stimulation relaxes the detrusor; alpha-1 activity contracts bladder neck/proximal urethral smooth muscle. |
| Somatic | S2-S4, Onuf's nucleus, via pudendal nerve. | Acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors contracts the external urethral sphincter and supports voluntary continence. |
| Afferents | Pelvic and other visceral pathways. | Stretch-sensitive A-delta fibres convey physiological filling; C-fibre pathways contribute to nociception and may become important after neurological injury. |

During storage, sympathetic and pudendal outflow promote detrusor relaxation and outlet closure while parasympathetic activity is suppressed. The guarding reflex increases external sphincter activity with rising abdominal pressure. During voiding, pontine coordination activates parasympathetic detrusor contraction and inhibits sympathetic/somatic outlet activity; urethral smooth muscle relaxation also involves nitrergic pathways.

Suprasacral spinal lesions may produce neurogenic detrusor overactivity with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia. Sacral/peripheral lesions may cause weak detrusor contraction and/or a weak outlet. Actual patterns vary with lesion, age and evolution: anatomical level alone cannot replace urodynamics. High storage pressure, poor compliance, reflux, infection and incomplete emptying threaten the upper tracts.

Treatment targets safe low-pressure storage and reliable emptying before cosmetic continence. Assess renal/bladder ultrasound, renal function, residuals, infection history and urodynamics. Clean intermittent catheterization (CIC) and bowel management frequently form the foundation; a drug that relaxes the detrusor may worsen residual urine without adequate emptying.

### (b) Drug classification and mechanisms - 5 marks

| Group / examples | Mechanism / role | Important limitations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Antimuscarinics: oxybutynin; selected tolterodine, solifenacin, propiverine or trospium | Block muscarinic signalling and reduce involuntary detrusor contraction; improve storage capacity and pressure. | Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, heat intolerance and retention; cognitive effects may occur. Age approval and formulation vary. |
| Beta-3 agonist: mirabegron | Activates beta-3 receptors to relax the detrusor during filling; alternative or add-on for storage dysfunction. | Monitor BP, pulse and residuals. US paediatric NDO approval is age >=3 years with formulation/weight-specific rules. |
| Botulinum toxin A, intradetrusor | Cleaves SNAP-25 and inhibits presynaptic acetylcholine release; reduces refractory neurogenic detrusor activity. | Delivered by cystoscopic injection; effect is temporary. UTI/retention and need for CIC must be discussed. |
| Alpha-1 blockers: selected tamsulosin, doxazosin or prazosin | Relax bladder-neck/proximal urethral smooth muscle to reduce outlet resistance in selected patients. | Off-label in many paediatric contexts, variable evidence; hypotension. Does not directly paralyse the external striated sphincter. |
| Striated sphincter relaxants: selected baclofen or diazepam | Central antispastic effects may reduce sphincter activity in selected neurological disorders. | Limited bladder-specific evidence, sedation and systemic effects; not routine first-line treatment. |
| Parasympathomimetic: bethanechol (historical) | Muscarinic agonism attempts to increase detrusor contraction in an underactive bladder. | Poor evidence and cholinergic adverse effects; not routine treatment and unsafe with unrelieved outlet obstruction. |

Oxybutynin is a common first antimuscarinic. Alternative oral or selected intravesical routes may be used by specialist teams when adverse effects limit treatment. Choose a drug from the measured storage/emptying pattern, not the label neurogenic bladder alone. Renal/bladder surveillance and repeat functional assessment remain necessary even when leakage improves.

Botulinum toxin is an escalation for inadequate response or intolerance to conservative treatment; dose limits differ by preparation and indication, so toxin units are not interchangeable. Outlet injections are distinct from detrusor injections. Surgery or augmentation may become necessary for persistent unsafe storage, but is outside this question's pharmacology focus.

Current-revision distinction: mirabegron approval for paediatric neurogenic detrusor overactivity does not imply approval for every child with idiopathic overactive bladder. Antibiotics treat documented symptomatic infection and are not drugs that restore bladder innervation; desmopressin reduces urine production but does not make an unsafe bladder compliant. Later 2023 guidance supports individualized medication with CIC and surveillance.

### References
- [CUA/PUC guideline on paediatric neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (2023; later update)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10581733/)
- [EAU/ESPU guideline, diagnostics and conservative management (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nau.24211)
- [FDA, mirabegron paediatric NDO approval (2021)](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USFDA/bulletins/2c98ff2)

### Illustration
Bladder innervation: storage, voiding and drug targets
The anatomy separates smooth detrusor/outlet targets from the striated external sphincter. Neurological lesion level does not reliably predict the final urodynamic pattern. Improved dryness alone does not prove safe storage pressure.

questions.title: Levels of evidence, randomized trials and cohort studies
questions.body_md:
Marks: 4 + 3 + 3
Discuss research studies under: (a) Hierarchy in level of evidence. (b) Randomised control trial (RCT). (c) Cohort studies.

### (a) Hierarchy of evidence - 4 marks

A level of evidence describes the likely protection against bias offered by a study design for a particular question. It is not a guarantee that its result is correct. State the framework and clinical question: hierarchies for treatment, diagnostic accuracy, prognosis and harms differ. The familiar treatment hierarchy is suitable for an examination overview.

| Traditional treatment hierarchy | Typical design | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Level I | Systematic review/meta-analysis of high-quality RCTs; individual high-quality RCTs in some systems. | Best design-based support for causal treatment effects when conduct and applicability are sound. |
| Level II | Lower-quality RCT or well-designed prospective comparative cohort, depending on the system. | Bias and confounding require explicit assessment. |
| Level III | Case-control or retrospective comparative studies in common surgical classifications. | Useful for associations and uncommon outcomes; vulnerable to selection/measurement bias. |
| Level IV | Case series and poor-quality observational evidence. | Describes experience; no reliable untreated/comparator counterfactual. |
| Level V | Expert opinion or mechanism-based reasoning without critical clinical outcome evidence. | Can inform practice when data are absent but is especially uncertain. |

This table is a broad surgical convention, not a verbatim Oxford numbering scheme. In the Oxford 2009 treatment framework, 1a is a homogeneous systematic review of RCTs, 1b an individual RCT with a narrow confidence interval, 2a a homogeneous review of cohort studies, 2b an individual cohort or low-quality RCT, 3a a review of case-control studies, 3b an individual case-control study, 4 case series/poor-quality observational studies and 5 expert opinion. Do not mix these labels silently.

Oxford 2011 uses question-specific levels 1-5 with downgrading for bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness or small effects, and possible upgrading for a large effect. A well-designed diagnostic cohort with blinded comparison to a reference standard may be more appropriate for a diagnostic question than an RCT. Prognosis commonly requires an inception cohort.

GRADE rates certainty across a body of evidence as high, moderate, low or very low and separately considers recommendation strength. A meta-analysis cannot repair biased primary data. Consistency, effect size, confidence intervals, harms, resource use and relevance to paediatric surgical patients must accompany the design label.

### (b) Randomized controlled trial - 3 marks

An RCT prospectively assigns eligible consenting participants to an intervention or comparator using a genuinely random sequence. Randomization balances measured and unmeasured prognostic factors on average. Allocation concealment prevents recruiters predicting the next assignment; blinding reduces performance and outcome-assessment bias after allocation. These are different safeguards.

Specify PICO, eligibility, primary outcome and follow-up before recruitment. Register the trial, obtain ethics approval and age-appropriate assent/parental permission, calculate sample size and use a justified randomization method such as computer-generated blocks with stratification where needed. Describe standard care and rescue treatment in both arms.

Analyse the primary effectiveness result by intention to treat: retain participants in their assigned group, with appropriate handling and sensitivity analysis for missing data. Report participant flow, crossovers, protocol deviations, effect estimates with confidence intervals and adverse events. In a surgical RCT, expertise, learning curves, centre effects and inability to blind the operating surgeon deserve attention; blinded outcome adjudication may still be possible.

Advantages include strong causal inference and reduction of confounding. Limitations include cost, time, rare-outcome power, restrictive eligibility, ethical constraints and loss to follow-up. Equipoise is essential. Random allocation does not guarantee balance in a small sample and is not the same as random population sampling.

### (c) Cohort studies - 3 marks

A cohort groups people by an exposure or characteristic and compares subsequent outcomes. In a prospective study, exposure is measured before follow-up outcomes occur. In a retrospective cohort, existing records reconstruct a defined cohort and its outcome experience; its conceptual direction is still exposure to outcome. A cohort may be population-based, registry-based or hospital-based.

Define an eligible source population and time zero, measure exposure consistently, select an appropriate comparison group, ascertain outcomes similarly and minimize losses. Record potential confounders before outcome assessment where possible. Report risks, incidence rates, risk ratios, rate ratios or hazard ratios with uncertainty; adjusted analyses may use regression, matching, stratification or weighting.

Example: follow children after neonatal bowel resection, comparing subsequent parenteral nutrition dependence by retained anatomy while accounting for underlying disease and baseline severity. This can study multiple outcomes and establish timing but cannot fully remove unmeasured confounding. Cohorts are useful for prognosis and uncommon exposures; they are inefficient for very rare outcomes without a very large population.

Common problems include confounding by indication, differential follow-up, inaccurate exposure/outcome recording and immortal-time bias if time zero is misaligned. Relative risk is (a/[a+b]) divided by (c/[c+d]) in a simple exposed/unexposed table. Case-control studies instead select by outcome and usually estimate odds ratios; do not describe them as retrospective cohorts merely because both use records.

### References
- [Oxford CEBM, levels of evidence (2009)](https://www.cebm.ox.ac.uk/resources/levels-of-evidence/oxford-centre-for-evidence-based-medicine-levels-of-evidence-march-2009)
- [Oxford CEBM, explanation of the 2011 levels](https://www.cebm.ox.ac.uk/resources/levels-of-evidence/explanation-of-the-2011-ocebm-levels-of-evidence)
- [Oxford CEBM, introductory document and question-specific appraisal](https://www.cebm.ox.ac.uk/resources/levels-of-evidence/levels-of-evidence-introductory-document)

### Illustration
RCT versus cohort: where does allocation occur?
Both designs move conceptually from exposure/intervention to outcomes. A retrospective cohort reconstructs that sequence from existing records; a case-control study selects participants by outcome. Random allocation is different from random sampling.

questions.title: Pyloric stenosis: biochemical disturbance and optimization
questions.body_md:
Marks: 5 + 5
Enumerate and discuss the changes in the acid-base and serum biochemistry in a case of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis of long duration. Discuss the pre-operative correction and optimization of the altered acid-base status and serum biochemistry in such cases.

### (a) Acid-base and biochemical changes - 5 marks

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes gastric outlet obstruction and repeated non-bilious vomiting. Prolonged loss of gastric hydrochloric acid produces hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, often accompanied by dehydration and total-body potassium depletion. The classic biochemical pattern is a late manifestation: early presentation may have normal electrolytes, and severe systemic illness may create a mixed acid-base disorder.

| Disturbance | Mechanism | Clinical consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raised bicarbonate / metabolic alkalosis | Loss of gastric H+; chloride depletion and reduced effective circulating volume impair renal bicarbonate excretion. | Alkalaemia, compensatory hypoventilation and peri-anaesthetic apnoea risk. |
| Hypochloraemia | Repeated chloride-rich gastric losses. | Sustains chloride-responsive alkalosis and guides replacement. |
| Potassium depletion +/- hypokalaemia | Gastrointestinal loss, intracellular shift with alkalosis and aldosterone-mediated renal K+ loss. | Weakness, ileus and arrhythmia risk; serum K+ may underestimate total-body deficit. |
| Sodium disturbance | Variable sodium loss and free-water intake/retention. | Often hyponatraemia, but sodium is not uniformly low. |
| Prerenal azotaemia | Reduced perfusion from dehydration. | Raised urea/creatinine, oliguria and reduced drug clearance. |
| Other findings | Haemoconcentration; possible starvation ketosis/hypoglycaemia; occasional indirect hyperbilirubinaemia. | Assess individually; jaundice can occur with the icteropyloric association. |

Initially, the kidney may excrete bicarbonate, giving alkaline urine. As volume and chloride depletion progress, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation increases distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen. With potassium depletion, hydrogen secretion is further favoured. The result can be paradoxical aciduria: acidic urine despite systemic metabolic alkalosis.

The maintenance of alkalosis therefore involves more than simply loss of acid. Low filtration, extracellular volume contraction, chloride depletion and potassium deficit prevent appropriate bicarbonate excretion. Replacing chloride and restoring effective circulating volume permits correction. Potassium replacement helps reverse renal hydrogen secretion once safe renal excretion is established.

Blood gas shows elevated bicarbonate with a compensatory rise in carbon dioxide; excessive hypoventilation, sepsis or aspiration can alter this pattern. Consider a mixed disorder if the gas is not consistent with simple compensation. Urinary chloride can support chloride depletion, but it is not required in every typical case and is affected by recent IV saline.

### (b) Pre-operative correction - 5 marks

Pyloromyotomy follows resuscitation and biochemical optimization. An obstructed but stable infant usually benefits from delaying anaesthesia until dehydration and alkalosis are corrected. Assess weight, feeding/vomiting duration, losses, perfusion, fontanelle, urine output and respiratory status; confirm the diagnosis by ultrasound and involve paediatric surgery and anaesthesia.

Keep the infant nil by mouth. Decompress the stomach with an NG/OG tube according to the surgical protocol, document aspirates and avoid unmeasured ongoing losses. Check glucose, sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, urea/creatinine and a blood gas when indicated. Monitor fluid balance, serial weight and electrolytes/gas during active correction.

If shock or significant perfusion impairment is present, give a 10 mL/kg aliquot of 0.9% saline and reassess; repeat only as clinically indicated under the local infant-resuscitation pathway. Then provide a calculated chloride-rich isotonic fluid regimen with glucose to meet maintenance, deficit and measured ongoing losses. The rate depends on dehydration, sodium and response; a fixed high rate is not appropriate for every infant.

Add potassium only after urine output and renal function have been assessed and the serum result reviewed. Never administer potassium as an IV bolus. Replace significant gastric aspirate losses in addition to maintenance/deficit treatment using an appropriate chloride-containing solution. Avoid bicarbonate: this is generally a chloride-responsive alkalosis, not bicarbonate deficiency.

| Readiness domain | Desired finding before anaesthesia |
| --- | --- |
| Clinical | Restored perfusion and hydration; adequate urine output; no ongoing shock or significant respiratory compromise. |
| Chloride | Usually >=100 mmol/L. |
| Bicarbonate / pH | Normalizing acid-base status; a published consensus uses bicarbonate <26 mmol/L and pH <=7.45. |
| Potassium / sodium / glucose | Within the treating unit's safe infant range. Consensus lower bounds: K+ >=3.5, Na+ >=132 and glucose >=4.0 mmol/L; these are not complete normal ranges. |
| Team / airway | Anaesthetic agreement, corrected relevant abnormalities and a plan for gastric emptying and aspiration prevention. |

Numerical criteria vary across centres; do not operate solely because one threshold has been crossed if the infant remains dehydrated or hypokalaemic. Some protocols accept a higher bicarbonate, whereas others target <25 or <26 mmol/L. Use the current local pathway and serial results. Cerebrospinal fluid alkalosis may lag behind plasma correction, supporting careful perioperative respiratory monitoring.

After biochemical correction and anaesthetic clearance, perform pyloromyotomy. Continue appropriate fluids and postoperative observation, with feeding progression according to the surgical pathway. Persistent vomiting should prompt clinical review rather than indefinite assumption of normal recovery. Exam emphasis: explain paradoxical aciduria and make chloride/volume restoration the centre of preoperative treatment.

### References
- [RCH clinical guideline, pyloric stenosis](https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Pyloric_stenosis/)
- [van den Bunder et al., Delphi consensus on preoperative care, Eur J Pediatr Surg 2020;30:497-504](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31958865/)
- [PIER Network, pre-operative care of infants with pyloric stenosis](https://www.piernetwork.org/guidelines-pyloric-stenosis.html)

### Illustration
Pyloric stenosis: why paradoxical aciduria develops
Initial urine may be alkaline; paradoxical aciduria is a later physiological response, not a requirement for diagnosis. Serum potassium can appear normal despite a total-body deficit. Do not use bicarbonate to treat chloride-responsive alkalosis.

questions.title: PET, surgical lasers and 3D reconstruction
questions.body_md:
Marks: 4 + 3 + 3
(a) PET scan. (b) Lasers in pediatric surgery. (c) 3 D reconstructions.

### (a) PET scan - 4 marks

Positron emission tomography is functional imaging using a positron-emitting radiotracer. After emission, positron-electron annihilation produces two approximately opposite 511-keV photons; coincidence detection permits reconstruction of tracer distribution. PET/CT adds anatomical localization and attenuation correction. PET/MRI combines metabolic information with MRI anatomy, with different acquisition and attenuation challenges.

18F-FDG is transported into metabolically active cells and phosphorylated, producing relative intracellular trapping. Uptake reflects glucose metabolism rather than malignancy specifically. Standardized uptake value is a semiquantitative measure affected by glucose, uptake time, body-size normalization, scanner/reconstruction and partial-volume effects; a single SUV cutoff cannot diagnose cancer reliably.

Paediatric uses include selected lymphoma staging/response assessment, assessment of FDG-avid sarcomas, investigation of suspected recurrent/metastatic disease and planning biopsy of heterogeneous lesions. Tracer choice depends on tumour biology. Many neuroblastomas are assessed with MIBG rather than routine FDG PET; FDG can have a role in selected MIBG-nonavid or discordant disease. PET does not replace pathology or tumour-specific staging.

Prepare with age-appropriate fasting and glucose assessment, avoiding strenuous activity and minimizing cold-induced brown-fat uptake. Maintain hydration, encourage voiding when appropriate and coordinate sedation with fasting and uptake needs. Use weight-appropriate administered activity and tailor the CT component to whether attenuation correction, localization or diagnostic CT is required. Avoid duplicate diagnostic CT examinations without a clinical reason.

False positives arise with inflammation, infection, healing and activated marrow/brown fat. False negatives occur in small lesions, low-avidity tumours, hyperglycaemia or inappropriate timing. Limitations include radiation, cost, access, motion and sedation burden. Interpretation must account for treatment timing and the clinical question; renal or urinary tracer excretion can obscure nearby lesions.

### (b) Lasers in paediatric surgery - 3 marks

LASER means light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Tissue effect depends on wavelength, chromophore absorption, energy density, pulse duration and exposure time. Energy may cut, vaporize, coagulate or fragment tissue. Selective photothermolysis targets a chromophore while limiting thermal diffusion when appropriate parameters are used.

| Laser / typical wavelength | Selected use | Important limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pulsed-dye, about 585-595 nm | Selected capillary malformations and superficial vascular lesions. | Requires lesion-specific assessment; not every vascular anomaly benefits. |
| CO2, 10,600 nm | Precise superficial cutting/vaporization in selected skin, mucosal or airway procedures. | Water absorption limits penetration but airway fire/thermal injury remain serious risks. |
| Nd:YAG, 1064 nm | Selected deeper coagulation applications. | Greater tissue penetration raises collateral injury risk. |
| Holmium:YAG, about 2100 nm | Endoscopic urinary stone fragmentation and selected urological applications. | Eye protection, fibre integrity and irrigation/visibility are essential. |

Advantages include precision and haemostasis in selected tissues; disadvantages include equipment cost, learning requirements, thermal injury, scarring, perforation and plume. Safety includes a trained team, wavelength-specific eye protection, smoke evacuation, controlled access, checked equipment and prevention of oxygen-enriched fire conditions. Airway laser use requires a specific anaesthetic/fire plan. Energy modality is chosen for the lesion, not because it is technologically newer.

### (c) Three-dimensional reconstruction - 3 marks

3D reconstruction converts cross-sectional imaging into a spatial representation for clinical interpretation or planning. Thin-slice CT or appropriate MRI data are segmented to identify structures, then processed by multiplanar reformatting, surface rendering or volume rendering. A segmented model may be used for virtual planning or exported for 3D printing; these are related but distinct products.

Applications include vascular mapping in congenital lung lesions, renal tumour relationships to vessels/collecting system, hepatobiliary anatomy, pelvic/urogenital malformations and complex craniofacial or orthopaedic deformity. A model can help plan resection planes, anticipate access and explain anatomy to the family or team. 3D displays in endoscopic surgery provide depth perception but are a separate concept from preoperative image reconstruction.

Workflow: define the surgical question; acquire clinically justified data; segment structures with expert review; construct and label the model; check it against source slices; then use it for planning. Verify vessel continuity, laterality, scale, missing small branches and registration error. A visually convincing model may still contain a segmentation error.

Benefits are improved spatial communication and potential assistance in complex cases. Limits include radiation/contrast if extra CT is obtained, cost, processing time, motion artefact and failure to represent tissue compliance or intraoperative distortion. Better visualization does not automatically establish improved outcomes. Preserve source imaging and validate anatomy rather than treating a printed model as ground truth.

Exam emphasis: for PET explain the tracer principle and limitations; for lasers link wavelength to tissue effect and safety; for 3D reconstruction describe the acquisition-to-validation workflow and concrete paediatric applications.

### References
- [SNMMI/EANM, paediatric 18F-FDG PET/CT oncology standard (2021)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33334912/)
- [SNMMI/EANM full procedure standard](https://jnm.snmjournals.org/content/jnumed/62/1/99.full.pdf)
- [FDA, medical lasers](https://www.fda.gov/radiation-emitting-products/surgical-and-therapeutic-products/medical-lasers)
- [Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, lasers in health care](https://www.ccohs.ca/oshanswers/phys_agents/lasers.html)
- [Preoperative 3D reconstruction images for paediatric tumours: advantages and drawbacks (2020), prospective observational study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32827349/)
- [NCI, paediatric CT radiation considerations](https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/causes-prevention/risk/radiation/pediatric-ct-scans)

### Illustration
Three technologies: signal, tissue effect and reconstruction
PET/CT reconstruction and preoperative 3D anatomical modelling are related imaging operations with different clinical aims. A surgical laser is a treatment energy source, not an imaging substitute. Technologies must answer a defined clinical question.
